Description:
Why
git-sync and the mirror pipeline send every ref tip as a have. Most tips are ancestors of other tips, so the have list is much larger than it needs to be. Large repos pay for this with extra negotiation round trips and megabytes of have lines.
What
ls-refs accepts a new vendor argument, entire-maximal. The server then marks each listed ref whose peeled commit no other listed ref reaches. The marked refs, deduplicated by the client, form a have set that implies the history of every listed ref.
gitutil.MaximalTips computes the set with reachability bitmaps. It checks fresh tips first, so a new push on top of packed history costs one walk.
The result is conservative. A tip is unmarked only when the server proves it reachable. A two-second budget, the walk frontier cap, a repo without a bitmap and non-commit tips all keep tips marked.
ref-prefix and hidden refs narrow the set that the marks are computed over. A client must list only refs that the other side also holds. Otherwise a marked tip that the other side lacks hides its ancestors from the fetch.
closureInto now checks the context before each commit read, so the budget holds on slow storage. This also applies to the existing merge-base callers.
Compatibility and rollout
This release accepts the argument but does not advertise it. Stateless HTTP v2 can send the capability request and the ls-refs request to different nodes, and an older node rejects an unknown argument. A later release passes lsrefs.WithMaximalAdvertised() after every node accepts the argument. Clients that do not send the argument see no change.
Observability
The ls-refs span records ls_refs.maximal. The reduction span records the method, the marked count, closure walks and evictions. Two counters explain extra marks: unchecked counts tips the budget skipped, and truncated counts walks that hit the frontier cap because of a stale bitmap.
Tests
gitutil: fresh-tip cost bound, no-bitmap fallback, exhausted budget, the frontier cap, non-commit tips, cancellation on both paths, a slow-storage budget test, and a random-DAG comparison with Independent.
server/gitrefs: marks over a packed repo with a bitmap, the ref-prefix scope, and peel interaction.
lsrefs: request decoding without the advertisement, the wire encoding and the capability string.
server/githttp: an HTTP integration test for the argument.
mise run lint:migrations does not run locally because clang rejects the macOS SDK. The other lint tasks pass.
Follow-ups
git-sync: send entire-maximal to the target, request only mirrored prefixes, and use the marked peeled hashes as haves. Fall back to all tips when the server does not advertise the feature.
Next release: advertise the feature with lsrefs.WithMaximalAdvertised().
Optional: a commit-graph fallback for repos without a bitmap.

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- **`RefScope.IndependentHistoryRefPrefixes` shrinks the haves of a relay fetch.** A relay fetch offers the source every target tip as a have. For refs that each carry their own history, such as one orphan history per session checkpoint, those tips cannot shorten the pack, and a repository with thousands of them sent thousands of have lines for a run that changed one branch. Under the named prefixes, a target ref is now offered only when the run updates it, as its own old value. Replicate and sync's incremental relay honor it. Sync's closure fetch for fast-forward checks and bootstrap still offer every tip. Which refs are synced or pruned does not change. Entries are literal prefixes of target ref names and must start with `refs/`; end a namespace with a slash. Naming refs that do share history keeps the copy complete but resends objects the target already holds, and the larger pack can hit a pack or request size limit.

### Changed

- Bumped `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6` and `github.com/go-git/go-billy/v6` to `v6.0.0-beta.1`, along with `testify` `v1.12.1` and the indirect dependencies (`golang.org/x/net` `v0.62.0`, `golang.org/x/sync` `v0.24.0`, `ProtonMail/go-crypto` `v1.5.2`, `cloudflare/circl` `v1.6.5`, `pjbgf/sha1cd` `v0.7.0`, `Microsoft/go-winio` `v0.6.4`, `spf13/pflag` `v1.0.10`). The Go toolchain stays at `1.27.3`, the current release.
- Moved `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6` and `github.com/go-git/go-billy/v6` past `v6.0.0-beta.1` to their `main` commits of 4 November 2026 (`bbee1d214130` and `3dcdd520bf27`), ahead of the next tagged release. go-git's tree walker now returns an error for a subtree it cannot read instead of ending the walk as if the tree were complete ([go-git/go-git#2555](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/issues/2555)). Packs cut off in the header, or with objects shorter than their declared size, are rejected with an error. `convert-sha256` decodes tree entry modes as git does: a regular file whose mode has an execute bit set but not the owner's, such as `100011`, now converts as `100644` where it used to convert as `100755`, so such a tree gets a different SHA-256 hash than an earlier version produced, and a tree with a zero-padded mode, which failed to decode, now converts.
- Refs whose name starts with a dash (`refs/heads/-foo`) are now mirrored instead of skipped. go-git `beta.1` dropped that rule from `ReferenceName.Validate` to match git's `check_refname_format`: git restricts a leading dash only when a branch or tag is created, and `git fetch` and `git clone` replicate such refs. `--map` accepts such names for the same reason. No ref name reaches a command line where a leading dash would be read as an option.

### Fixed

- **A branch whose new tip the target already holds under another ref now fast-forwards instead of failing the sync.** The planning fetch names every target ref as a have, so the source prunes such a tip from the pack and the ancestry check aborted the run with `load source commit …: object not found`. A mirror of NixOS/nixpkgs hit this whenever `nixos-unstable` advanced to a commit `master` had already delivered. A check the pruned store cannot settle is now resolved with one tree:0 commit-graph fetch of that tip against the ref's own target hash: a real fast-forward updates, and a rewind blocks as `not an ancestor`. A source that cannot serve that fetch (protocol v1, no filter support) leaves the ref blocked with the reason instead of crashing. Builds on [#79](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/79).
- **`BootstrapLogger` now receives the bootstrap planning and progress lines.** They went only to the `-v` stderr log, so an embedder saw the GitHub size lookup and then nothing until the first checkpoint upload. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. A push the target refused or timed out, and resume markers left on the target, go at Warn; a push git-sync stops itself at its byte budget and then splits stays at Info, so a successful bootstrap logs no warnings. Lines logged once per branch (subsumed by trunk, already on target) go at Debug, so a repository with thousands of branches does not emit thousands of Info records per attempt. Error text from the target is sanitized. `-v` shows every line it showed before. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))
- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.
- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.
- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.
- SSH fetches from GitHub intermittently failed with `update object storage: empty packfile`. The SSH transport wrote the request and closed stdin while the server was still streaming its ref advertisement (36 MB for `NixOS/nixpkgs`), and GitHub sometimes dropped a request that arrived that early. The request is now sent only after the advertisement is read, which is what `git` does. On the old code, 2 of 4 runs against `git@github.com:NixOS/nixpkgs.git` failed; with the change, 7 of 7 passed.
- Errors from closing an upload-pack stream (the ssh exit status and the remote's stderr) were dropped in `fetchToStoreV1` and `fetchToStoreV2`, because `CheckClose` wrote to a shadowed `err`. They are now joined into the returned error.

I added `entire-maximal` support to git-sync. It won't do anything in production yet, because the deployed entiredb accepts the argument but doesn't advertise it. git-sync only sends it when the target advertises it, so it starts working once entiredb passes `lsrefs.WithMaximalAdvertised()`. Tests and lint pass, including new tests that fail if the reduction is turned off. Nothing is committed yet.

**What it does**
- Once per run, git-sync asks the target over upload-pack v2 for `ls-refs entire-maximal`. It only asks for the namespaces the run mirrors (`refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/`, or `refs/` with `--all-refs`), or the `--include-ref-prefix` values if set. That follows the server's rule to list only refs the source also holds.
- Refs the target didn't mark are dropped from the haves. This applies to sync's planning fetch, sync's incremental relay, and replicate. Bootstrap is unchanged.
- Fewer haves can make a pack bigger, never incomplete. The worst case is that the source lacks a marked commit and resends history the target already has.

**Choices you may want to revisit**
- **When haves are dropped:** only if every marked ref is still at the hash it had in the listing. Replicate re-reads the target mid-run, after its own pushes, so a moved marked ref means that fetch sends every tip instead of guessing.
- **When git-sync doesn't ask at all:** `--protocol v1`, a target with fewer than 2 refs, and SSH targets. An SSH server that rejects `GIT_PROTOCOL` would send back its whole v0 ref list, which can be megabytes. HTTP and the `entire://` helper answer v2 with a short capability list.
- **Failures:** a failed listing is only logged at debug level (`-v`) and the run continues with every tip as a have.

**Changed files**
- `internal/gitproto/maximal.go`: `ListMaximalTips`, `MaximalTips.Reduce`, `ErrMaximalUnsupported`.
- `internal/syncer/maximal.go`: the once-per-run lookup and `fetchHaves`.
- `internal/syncer/syncer.go`: three call sites switched over.
- Tests:

  - The fake test server can now mark refs, so end-to-end tests cover sync and replicate, an unadvertised target, and `--protocol v1`.

**No risk to the comparison, but yes, we now list the target refs twice.**

**The comparison isn't affected.** The planner still compares source refs against the target's full list, which comes from the receive-pack advertisement. The `entire-maximal` listing feeds only one thing: the `have` lines sent to the source during the fetch (`syncer.go:1093`, `:1652`, `:1692`). `Reduce` builds a new map and never changes the target's ref list, so create, update and delete decisions are exactly what they were. If the maximal listing were wrong, the worst case is that the source sends history the target already has. Nothing gets skipped or deleted.

**There are two listings.** Each run that qualifies now makes:
1. The existing receive-pack ref advertisement. This is the full list, and it also carries the push capabilities, so we still need it.
2. An upload-pack v2 capability probe plus one ls-refs request, limited to the mirrored prefixes. This is two more round trips and a second copy of those refs. On entiredb it took about 0.6s for heads and tags.

It runs at most once per run, and is skipped under protocol v1, for SSH targets, and for targets with fewer than two refs. We can't use the ls-refs listing in place of the advertisement, because pushing needs the receive-pack connection and its capabilities.

**The two lists can disagree if refs move in between.** `Reduce` handles that conservatively:
- **A marked ref differs between the lists** (missing, or at another hash): nothing is dropped and every tip stays a have.
- **An unmarked ref is at a different hash:** that ref is kept.
- **A ref is new or deleted in between:** it's either not covered by the listing, so it's kept, or it's marked and missing from the haves, so nothing is dropped.

A ref is dropped only when every marked ref matches between the two lists, which is exactly the case the server's proof covers.

**Whether it pays off:** the extra request costs about 0.6s and saved about 10% of the haves on entiredb. That's a modest win there. It's bigger for targets with many tips that build on each other, where the have lines make up a real share of the fetch.

Finding (medium, confidence ~0.8) — internal/gitproto/maximal.go, Reduce
- Trigger: a marked target tip the source no longer holds, sitting on top of an unmarked ref. Examples are a branch deleted on the source and not pruned, or a force-pushed branch whose old tip the source has garbage-collected.

I fixed the finding by asking the source to confirm each marked tip before reducing. All tests and lint pass. The change is uncommitted in the worktree, so trail #2808 doesn't have it yet.

**What it does.** Before dropping any haves, git-sync now checks that the source holds every marked tip:
- **Advertised tips:** a marked tip at a hash the source advertises counts as held.
- **The rest:** git-sync asks the source in one extra request: a v2 `fetch` with `wait-for-done`, the unconfirmed tips as haves, no wants and no `done`. The source replies with an ACK for each tip it holds and sends no pack.
- **Fallback:** if any tip isn't ACKed, or the source can't be asked (protocol v1, or no `wait-for-done`), that run offers every tip as a have, as before the feature.

In your example, X isn't ACKed, so the haves stay C and X and the pack is just D and X'.

**One caveat about the ACKs.** Git doesn't ACK a have that is the direct parent of an earlier ACKed one. Marked tips never reach each other, so this doesn't affect us normally. If the server's 2s budget leaves extra refs marked, the cost is a skipped reduction for that run, never a bigger pack.

**Checked against real servers:**
- Local git 2.50 `upload-pack` answers that request with an acknowledgments section and no pack.
- GitHub advertises `fetch=shallow wait-for-done filter`. I sent a hand-built request to `github.com/go-git/go-git` with `main`, a tag, and a made-up hash. It ACKed the first two, skipped the fake, and sent no pack.

**Cost.** The one extra request to the source happens only when a marked tip isn't advertised, which is usually a branch that moved since the last run. In a typical mirror run that's one extra source request per run.

**Tests:**
- `TargetOnlyTipCostsBytesOnly` became `TargetOnlyTipKeepsEveryTip`.
- New `ForcePushedTipKeepsEveryTip` recreates your example: the target's feature tip exists only on the target, master moves, and feature is rewritten. It asserts every tip stays a have and the mirror ends correct.
- New `SourceWithoutWaitForDoneKeepsEveryTip` covers a source that can't be asked.
- Unit tests cover `SourceHolds`: the request it sends (no wants, no `done`), NAK, a source that can't be asked, and refusing a response that announces a pack.
- The shrink test now asserts one listing and one source request per run. That assertion was supposed to go in last round, but my edit didn't match the file and I missed it; it's in now.
- With the source check disabled, the new tests fail.

The fake server now advertises `wait-for-done` and answers these requests the way git does, and the recorder that counts haves ignores them. I also updated the CHANGELOG entry.
